criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 49-yr-old woman comes to the emergency department because of chest pain. She says she
was in her usual state of health until the day before, when she awoke at 6 am with the sudden
onset of sharp left-sided chest pain. Pain has been constant and radiates to the center of her
chest. It is not worsened by exertion, movement, food, activity, or respiration. She also had
shortness of breath and chills but no cough, nausea, or diaphoresis. She took 400 mg of
naproxen without relief. The pain has persisted, prompting her to come to the emergency
department now. She has never had chest pain before this episode and has no known history of
cardiac or pulmonary disease.

Review of Systems:
General: Chills as noted in History of Present Illness. She thought she had a fever but did not
take her temperature.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: No recent URI symptoms.

Pulmonary: As per History of Present Illness.

Cardiovascular: Chest pain as per History of Present Illness. No palpitations or syncope. She
has noted dyspnea with climbing stairs since chest pain began; dyspnea resolves quickly with
rest and is not worsened by lying flat.

Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. Appetite and bowel movements are
normal.

Genitourinary: Minimal spotting after recent menses.

Musculoskeletal: She has no current musculoskeletal symptoms, although she has noted
intermittent left leg swelling and discomfort for the past year. There is no history of injury or

recent immobilization. The last time she had swelling and discomfort in her left leg was about 10
days ago.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Menorrhagia due to uterine fibroids, with secondary iron-deficiency anemia;
endometriosis; right breast fibroadenoma. No history of blood clots or clotting disorder.

Surgical history: Laparoscopy and lysis of adhesions for endometriosis; tubal ligation; excision
of breast fibroadenoma.

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Mother was recently diagnosed with stage IV colon carcinoma; brother has
schizophrenia.

Social history: No tobacco or alcohol use; former cocaine and heroin use (quit both more than
20 yr ago); works for the hospital in the food services department. No recent travel.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Appears anxious and in some pain. No cyanosis or respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature 36.8° C
Pulse 107 beats/min
BP right arm 130/72 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
O2 saturation 96% on room air

Skin: No lesions or rashes.

HEENT: Mucus membranes moist, no oral lesions, patent nares.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No crackles or wheezes.

Cardiovascular: Elevated rate, regular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. No tenderness to
palpation. No jugular venous distention. Normal carotid pulse.

Gastrointestinal: bdomen nontender and nondistended with normal bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Uterus palpated just below the umbilicus. No blood in vaginal vault.

Musculoskeletal: No joint deformity, full range of motion without pain. Lower extremities: no
swelling, erythema, or tenderness.

Neurologic: Cranial nerves intact; muscle strength and sensation intact throughout.

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate laboratory testing return and show:
Serum D-dimer level: 395 ng/mL [2.16 nmol/L]
Hemoglobin: 9.7 g/dL
Platelets: 330,000/mcL
WBC: 10,600/mcL
Serum troponin I level: 0.05 ng/mL [0.05 mcg/L]

ECG is obtained and is shown.

CT scan of the chest with IV contrast is obtained and shows a filling defect in bilateral upper and
lower segmental pulmonary arteries on pulmonary arterial phase.
winner_protocol:
Age: 49  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Acute onset of sharp left-sided chest pain radiating to the center of the chest, associated with shortness of breath and chills; pain is constant, not pleuritic or exertional, and unrelieved by naproxen.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute chest pain, dyspnea, and chills. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrates bilateral segmental filling defects, confirming acute pulmonary embolism (PE). She is hemodynamically stable (BP 130/72 mm Hg, HR 107 bpm, O2 saturation 96% on room air) but tachycardic. Risk factors include intermittent left leg swelling (suggestive of prior DVT), menorrhagia with iron-deficiency anemia, uterine fibroids, and endometriosis. The normal D-dimer (395 ng/mL) does not exclude PE; CT is diagnostic. Differential considerations include acute coronary syndrome (troponin normal, ECG not shown but no ischemic changes described), pneumonia (clear lungs, no fever), and musculoskeletal pain (no exacerbation with movement). The main challenge is balancing anticoagulation against her bleeding risk (anemia, menorrhagia).  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (diagnosis confirmed by CT; no additional urgent diagnostic tests required).  
Conclusion: Acute bilateral segmental pulmonary embolism in a hemodynamically stable patient with underlying iron-deficiency anemia and menorrhagia, likely secondary to DVT.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations: Admit to hospital for initiation of therapeutic anticoagulation (e.g., LMWH or unfractionated heparin) with close monitoring of hemoglobin and signs of bleeding. Perform lower extremity venous ultrasound to confirm DVT. Consult gynecology for management of menorrhagia and uterine fibroids. Initiate iron supplementation for anemia. After the acute phase, consider a hypercoagulability workup and malignancy screening (given family history of colon cancer). Monitor for anticoagulation-related bleeding, especially vaginal bleeding; consider dose adjustment or alternative agents if bleeding occurs.  
Notes: D-dimer was normal but is not reliable in this setting; CT is definitive. Anticoagulation is indicated despite bleeding risk; use caution and monitor closely. The palpable uterus below the umbilicus suggests significant fibroids, increasing bleeding risk.

Vignette:
A 72-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and recent urinary tract infection treated with oral antibiotics presents with 2 days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake. His wife reports he has been increasingly lethargic and today was unable to recognize her. On examination, he is obtunded, with warm, flushed skin. Vital signs: T 39.4C, HR 122, RR 26, BP 76/44 (MAP 55), SpO2 93% on room air. Suprapubic tenderness is present with a distended bladder. Foley catheter insertion yields 800 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine. Labs: WBC 24,800/mcL with 22% bands, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.2), lactate 5.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 48 ng/mL, platelets 82,000/mcL. Urinalysis shows too numerous to count WBC and bacteria. SOFA score is 11. Blood and urine cultures are obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation are initiated.
winner_protocol:
Age: 72  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Worsening confusion, fever, decreased oral intake, lethargy, and inability to recognize wife, with obtundation and hypotension.  
Analysis: The patient presents with septic shock (hypotension, lactate 5.8, SOFA 11) secondary to urosepsis, evidenced by fever, suprapubic tenderness, distended bladder, cloudy foul-smelling urine, pyuria, and elevated procalcitonin. Acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.2 from baseline 1.2), thrombocytopenia (platelets 82,000), and bandemia (22% bands) support severe systemic infection. The obtundation and warm flushed skin suggest distributive shock. Differential includes other sources of sepsis (pneumonia, intra-abdominal) but urinary source is most likely given the clinical and laboratory findings. Urinary obstruction (e.g., from BPH) may be contributing and requires evaluation.  
Required diagnostic/tests: Renal ultrasound (to assess for obstruction/abscess), repeat lactate, blood and urine cultures (already obtained), consider CT abdomen/pelvis if obstruction or abscess suspected, continuous hemodynamic monitoring, and serial CBC/creatinine/coagulation studies.  
Conclusion: Septic shock due to urosepsis with acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and altered mental status, requiring aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, source control, and intensive care.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency  
Recommendations: Continue IV fluid resuscitation (crystalloids) with reassessment of hemodynamics; initiate vasopressors (norepinephrine) if hypotension persists despite fluids; ensure broad-spectrum antibiotics cover gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem) and consider adding vancomycin if MRSA risk; obtain urology consultation for possible obstruction or need for drainage (e.g., nephrostomy if hydronephrosis); monitor urine output and renal function; correct coagulopathy if active bleeding or invasive procedures planned; admit to ICU for close monitoring; repeat lactate and reassess SOFA score; consider stress-dose steroids if refractory shock; evaluate for disseminated intravascular coagulation and manage accordingly.  
Notes: None

Age: 38  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Sudden onset severe vertigo, diplopia, difficulty swallowing, dysarthria, left Horner syndrome, right limb ataxia, left facial and right body pain/temperature loss, absent left gag reflex.  
Analysis: The patient presents with acute posterior circulation stroke syndrome (lateral medullary / Wallenberg syndrome) with crossed sensory loss, Horner, ataxia, and bulbar signs. CT head is negative for hemorrhage, and CTA confirms left vertebral artery occlusion. NIHSS 12 indicates moderate-severe deficit. The occlusion is a large vessel occlusion in the posterior circulation, making the patient a candidate for endovascular thrombectomy. Differential includes basilar artery occlusion, vertebral artery dissection, or cardioembolism; however, the CTA finding is definitive for left vertebral occlusion. Time from onset is 90 minutes, well within thrombectomy window.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CT perfusion or MRI (DWI/PWI) to assess penumbra and infarct core; conventional cerebral angiography if proceeding with thrombectomy; baseline labs (CBC, coagulation profile, renal function, glucose) and ECG.  
Conclusion: Acute ischemic stroke in the posterior circulation due to left vertebral artery occlusion, presenting as lateral medullary syndrome. Emergent revascularization is indicated.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  
Recommendations: Urgent evaluation for mechanical thrombectomy given confirmed large vessel occlusion and short time from onset. Administer IV thrombolysis if no contraindications (within 4.5 hours). Obtain CT perfusion or MRI to confirm salvageable tissue. Proceed to endovascular thrombectomy if technically feasible. Monitor airway closely due to dysphagia and absent gag reflex; consider elective intubation if aspiration risk is high. Manage blood pressure per stroke guidelines (avoid aggressive lowering). Investigate etiology (dissection vs embolic) with vessel wall imaging or echocardiography after acute treatment.  
Notes: None

Interprets noncontrast computed tomography for hemorrhage and early ischemic change, and computed tomographic angiography for the site and extent of large vessel occlusion in the anterior or posterior circulation. Assesses vessel anatomy, collateral supply, and features of dissection, and judges whether mechanical thrombectomy is technically feasible and likely to benefit the patient.

tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[2]
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[4]
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[5]
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

[6]
tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Age: 68
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive dyspnea on exertion, lower extremity edema, orthopnea, cough, wheezing, and 3-kg weight gain in the setting of recent heart failure diagnosis, with a fat pad biopsy showing Congo red-positive amyloid deposits.
Analysis: The patient presents with worsening heart failure symptoms (dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, weight gain) and signs of right- and left-sided congestion (JVD 12 cm, bibasilar crackles, S3, hepatomegaly, pitting edema to thighs). Echocardiography shows preserved LVEF (55%) with severe concentric LV hypertrophy and a restrictive diastolic filling pattern (E/A > 2, biatrial enlargement), which is characteristic of infiltrative cardiomyopathy. The fat pad biopsy demonstrates amorphous extracellular deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining, confirming amyloidosis. The history of MGUS, macroglossia, autonomic symptoms (orthostatic dizziness, syncope, erectile dysfunction), and low blood pressure (92/64 mm Hg) despite volume overload strongly suggest AL (light chain) amyloidosis with cardiac, autonomic, and possibly renal involvement. The differential includes transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, but the MGUS background and macroglossia favor AL. Other causes of HFpEF (hypertensive heart disease, valvular disease) are less likely given the biopsy-proven amyloid. The low-voltage ECG (unchanged) and elevated BNP (1420 pg/mL) with mild troponin elevation support cardiac amyloid involvement. The main task now is to confirm the amyloid subtype, assess the plasma cell clone, and stage cardiac and renal disease to guide therapy.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum and urine immunofixation; serum free light chain assay; bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry and FISH for plasma cell dyscrasia; mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry on the fat pad biopsy tissue to confirm amyloid subtype (AL vs ATTR); cardiac staging biomarkers (NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity troponin); renal assessment (serum creatinine, eGFR, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio); ECG and echocardiography (already obtained, but repeat as clinically indicated).
Conclusion: AL (light chain) amyloidosis with predominant cardiac involvement (restrictive cardiomyopathy with preserved EF), autonomic dysfunction, and probable early renal involvement, arising in a patient with known MGUS. The biopsy-proven amyloid, macroglossia, and MGUS history make AL amyloidosis the leading diagnosis, requiring urgent hematologic evaluation and staging.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology
Recommendations: 1) Confirm AL amyloidosis: order serum and urine immunofixation, serum free light chain assay, and bone marrow biopsy with plasma cell studies; perform mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry on the fat pad biopsy to distinguish AL from ATTR amyloid. 2) Stage cardiac involvement with NT-proBNP and high-sensitivity troponin; assess renal involvement with creatinine, eGFR, and urine protein quantification. 3) Refer promptly to hematology-oncology for plasma cell-directed therapy (e.g., bortezomib-based regimen) once AL is confirmed; avoid agents with significant cardiac toxicity. 4) Manage heart failure cautiously given hypotension (BP 92/64 mm Hg): use judicious diuresis with close monitoring of volume status and renal function; avoid aggressive preload reduction that could precipitate hypotension. 5) Monitor for arrhythmias (history of paroxysmal AF) and consider anticoagulation management in the context of amyloid cardiomyopathy. 6) Evaluate autonomic symptoms (orthostatic dizziness, syncope) and consider fall precautions; assess for carpal tunnel syndrome or other soft tissue involvement. 7) Coordinate multidisciplinary care with cardiology, hematology, and nephrology.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old obese man with a BMI of 34 presents with a 6-month history of persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation despite taking omeprazole 20 mg daily. He reports the heartburn is worse after large meals and when lying down, and he frequently wakes at night with a sour taste in his mouth and occasional coughing. He has tried elevating the head of his bed and avoiding late meals with only partial relief. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, or hematemesis. He drinks two to three beers on weekends and does not smoke. On examination, vital signs are normal. He is an obese man in no acute distress. Abdominal exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. His dentist has noted enamel erosion on posterior teeth.
winner_protocol:
Age: 50  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation despite omeprazole 20 mg daily, with nocturnal symptoms, coughing, and dental enamel erosion.  
Analysis: The patient has classic GERD symptoms that are refractory to standard-dose PPI therapy. Supporting factors include obesity (BMI 34), symptom exacerbation with large meals and recumbency, nocturnal regurgitation with sour taste and cough, and posterior enamel erosion on dental exam. The absence of alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis) makes an urgent complication less likely. However, refractory symptoms warrant evaluation for inadequate acid suppression, poor compliance, or alternative diagnoses such as eosinophilic esophagitis, functional heartburn, or anatomical abnormalities (e.g., hiatal hernia). Extraesophageal manifestations (cough, enamel erosion) further support significant reflux burden.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upper endoscopy (EGD) to evaluate for esophagitis, Barrett’s esophagus, or other mucosal pathology; esophageal pH monitoring (if EGD is normal) to confirm ongoing acid reflux; esophageal manometry (if pH monitoring is considered or to rule out motility disorders).  
Conclusion: Refractory GERD with extraesophageal manifestations, likely due to inadequate acid suppression or anatomical factors; requires further diagnostic evaluation and optimized therapy.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology  
Recommendations: Optimize PPI therapy (e.g., increase to 40 mg daily or split dosing), consider adding a nighttime H2 blocker for breakthrough symptoms, and reinforce lifestyle measures (weight loss, smaller meals, avoid eating 3 hours before bedtime, elevate head of bed). Refer for upper endoscopy to assess for erosive esophagitis, Barrett’s esophagus, or other pathology. If endoscopy is normal, consider esophageal pH monitoring to confirm reflux burden. Also consider testing for H. pylori if not previously done, as it may influence management.  
Notes: None

criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

winner_protocol:
Age: 28  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Pain and erythema on the palmar surface of the left index finger after accidental contact with a hot pan, with no blistering, numbness, or limited range of motion.  
Analysis: The patient presents with a superficial (first-degree) thermal burn of the left index finger. Key findings supporting this diagnosis include diffuse erythema without blistering or blanching, intact skin, tenderness, warmth, capillary refill <2 seconds, and preserved sensation and range of motion. The immediate cooling with water was appropriate. Differential considerations include a superficial partial-thickness burn (which would typically show blistering) and a deeper burn (which would show blanching, reduced capillary refill, or sensory loss) – both are excluded by the examination. The affected area is small (estimated <1% TBSA) and involves only the palmar aspect of one finger, with no functional impairment. No systemic symptoms or signs of infection are present.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None.  
Conclusion: Superficial (first-degree) thermal burn of the left index finger, limited to the palmar surface, with intact skin and normal neurovascular function. This is a minor, self-limited injury.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  
Recommendations: Continue cool compresses or cool running water for 10–15 minutes as needed for pain relief. Apply a soothing moisturizer or aloe vera gel to the affected area. Use oral analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) as needed for pain. Keep the area clean and dry; avoid tight dressings or bandages that might restrict circulation. Monitor for the development of blistering, increased pain, redness, swelling, or discharge, which would suggest a deeper burn or infection – if these occur, seek medical evaluation. No specific referral is required at this time.  
Notes: None.

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

winner_protocol:
Age: 20  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Bilateral itchy, watery eyes for 3 days, starting after spring pollen increase, in a patient with known seasonal allergies.  
Analysis: The presentation is classic for allergic conjunctivitis: bilateral itching, watery discharge, conjunctival injection, mild chemosis, and absence of pain, photophobia, purulent discharge, or vision changes. The clear watery discharge and lack of preauricular lymphadenopathy argue against viral or bacterial conjunctivitis. The temporal association with pollen and personal history of atopy strongly support an allergic etiology. No red flags (pain, photophobia, reduced vision) are present, so urgent ophthalmology referral is not indicated. Differential considerations include viral conjunctivitis (typically unilateral, may have preauricular node, often with URI symptoms) and bacterial conjunctivitis (purulent, sticky discharge), but these are less consistent with the history and exam.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical diagnosis; slit lamp examination optional if available but not required).  
Conclusion: Acute seasonal allergic conjunctivitis in a young woman with known atopy.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology  
Recommendations: Advise allergen avoidance (stay indoors during peak pollen times, keep windows closed, use air conditioning, wear wraparound sunglasses outdoors). Apply cold compresses to the eyes for symptomatic relief. Use preservative-free artificial tears as needed. Recommend over-the-counter antihistamine eye drops (e.g., ketotifen 0.025% twice daily) or oral antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine or loratadine) as first-line therapy. Instruct the patient to start her usual seasonal allergy medications if previously effective. If symptoms persist beyond 1–2 weeks, worsen, or any red flags develop (eye pain, photophobia, reduced vision), she should seek medical evaluation. No antibiotics are indicated. General hand hygiene is reasonable but not specifically required for allergic conjunctivitis.  
Notes: None

Vignette: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-day history of lower abdominal pain. She is 18 weeks pregnant by dates. The patient describes the pain as sharp, steady, and radiating across her lower abdomen bilaterally. Last night she developed new nausea and vomiting. She has not been able to keep down any food or drink this morning. She had a normal bowel movement yesterday. She says she felt cold and shivering this morning, followed by feeling warm; however, she did not check her temperature. She denies vaginal bleeding.
Review of Systems:
General: Patient feels generally weak and ill but was in her usual state of health until 3 days ago. She has gained approximately 5 lbs (2.3 kg) in the pregnancy so far.

Skin: She denies rash.

HEENT: Her mouth feels dry. No headache, nasal congestion, or sore throat.

Pulmonary: She denies cough or shortness of breath.

Cardiovascular: She denies chest pain or palpitations.

Age: 26 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: 3-day history of sharp, steady lower abdominal pain radiating bilaterally, with new nausea/vomiting, fever, and urinary symptoms in an 18-week pregnant patient.  
Analysis: The patient is an 18-week pregnant woman presenting with fever (38.8°C), tachycardia (120 bpm), bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness, and lower abdominal tenderness. Urinalysis shows pyuria (30-50 WBC/hpf), positive nitrites, leukocyte esterase, bacteria, and blood, with ketones indicating dehydration. These findings strongly support acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy. The absence of cervical motion tenderness, closed cervical os, and normal fetal heart rate argue against preterm labor or pelvic inflammatory disease. Differential includes appendicitis, ovarian torsion, renal colic, and round ligament pain, but the urinary findings and CVA tenderness are diagnostic. The patient is dehydrated (dry mucous membranes, ketones, inability to tolerate oral intake) and has systemic inflammatory response (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis), placing her at risk for sepsis and obstetric complications.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures, urine culture and sensitivity, serum lactate, complete blood count with differential, basic metabolic profile (repeat), and continuous fetal heart rate monitoring. No additional imaging is needed beyond the already performed renal/bladder ultrasound (which showed no hydronephrosis).  
Conclusion: Acute pyelonephritis in an 18-week pregnant patient with systemic symptoms, dehydration, and early sepsis criteria, requiring urgent hospitalization and intravenous therapy.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology  
Recommendations: Admit to hospital for intravenous hydration (e.g., normal saline bolus) and intravenous antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone 1-2 g daily or cefazolin, with consideration of local resistance patterns; avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines in pregnancy). Obtain blood and urine cultures before antibiotic administration. Administer antiemetics (e.g., ondansetron) as needed. Monitor maternal vital signs, urine output, and fetal heart rate. Consult obstetrics for ongoing management. Reassess for signs of sepsis (lactate, blood pressure) and consider early goal-directed therapy if hemodynamic instability develops. Discharge planning includes oral antibiotics (e.g., cephalexin) after clinical improvement, with close outpatient follow-up.  
Notes: Pregnancy increases the risk of complications from pyelonephritis, including preterm labor, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and sepsis. Avoid nephrotoxic agents and ensure antibiotics are pregnancy-safe. If the patient develops hypotension or worsening organ dysfunction, escalate to intensive care.

Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.

The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

winner_protocol:
Age: 10 years old  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Frequent nausea and dizziness during car rides, especially on winding roads, resolving within 15–20 minutes after stopping the vehicle.  
Analysis: The symptoms are clearly triggered by motion (car rides) and resolve with cessation of motion. The girl reports partial relief with front-seat sitting and looking out the window. She denies vomiting, hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or symptoms outside car rides. Physical examination, including neurological and otoscopic exams, is entirely normal. This presentation is classic for motion sickness (kinetosis). Differential considerations include vestibular disorders (e.g., benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood) and migraine-associated vertigo, but the absence of headache, hearing loss, gait disturbance, and symptoms at rest, along with the consistent trigger and resolution, make these unlikely. No red flags are present.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Benign recurrent motion sickness in a healthy 10-year-old child, with no evidence of underlying neurological or otologic pathology.  
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  
Recommendations: Counsel the family on preventive measures: have the child sit in the front seat, focus on a fixed horizon point, avoid reading or screen use during travel, and take frequent breaks on long trips. Consider graded habituation by gradually increasing exposure to motion. For significant symptoms, prophylactic medication (e.g., dimenhydrinate or scopolamine) may be used before travel, with appropriate pediatric dosing. Reassure the parents that this is a benign, self-limited condition. Advise follow-up if symptoms worsen, occur outside car rides, or new symptoms (headache, hearing loss, vertigo at rest) develop.  
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 50-year-old man presents with intermittent burning sensation in the substernal area that he has experienced occasionally over the past several weeks. The burning typically occurs 30 to 60 minutes after large meals, particularly those that are spicy or high in fat. The discomfort is relieved within minutes by over-the-counter antacids. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. He has no cardiac history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. There is no epigastric tenderness. Cardiac exam is unremarkable.
winner_protocol:
Age: 50
Sex: Male
Complaint: Intermittent substernal burning sensation occurring 30–60 minutes after large meals (especially spicy or high-fat), relieved within minutes by over-the-counter antacids.
Analysis: The substernal burning is temporally linked to meals, occurs in a postprandial window (30–60 min), and is promptly relieved by antacids — classic features of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Cardiac ischemia typically produces exertional pressure or discomfort relieved by rest or nitrates, is not relieved by antacids, and is not usually triggered by specific meal content. The patient has no cardiac history, normal vital signs, an unremarkable cardiac exam, and no alarm symptoms (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, melena). The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no epigastric tenderness. The strongest supporting facts are the meal relationship, antacid response, and absence of cardiac risk factors or alarm features. Main differential considerations include GERD (most likely), peptic ulcer disease, functional dyspepsia, and less likely cardiac ischemia or esophageal motility disorder. Given the clear response to antacids and lack of red-flag symptoms, a cardiac cause is very unlikely.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None immediately required. An empiric trial of acid suppression (PPI) and lifestyle modification is appropriate. If symptoms persist despite therapy or alarm features develop, upper endoscopy is indicated.
Conclusion: This is a classic presentation of gastroesophageal reflux disease. Cardiac ischemia is unlikely given the strong meal association, antacid responsiveness, normal exam, and absence of cardiac history. Management is non-emergent and centers on lifestyle modification and empiric acid suppression.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Recommend lifestyle modifications: avoid large, spicy, and high-fat meals; eat smaller, more frequent meals; avoid eating 2–3 hours before bedtime; elevate the head of the bed; and pursue weight loss if overweight. Start an empiric PPI (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg daily) for 4–8 weeks. If symptoms resolve, continue as needed and consider step-down therapy. If symptoms persist, recur after treatment, or if alarm symptoms (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding) develop, refer for upper endoscopy. Although cardiac cause is unlikely, advise the patient to seek immediate care if he develops exertional chest pressure, radiation to the arm or jaw, diaphoresis, or dyspnea.
Notes: None

Diagnosis10: Diverticular disease of large intestine without perforation or abscess
Vignette: A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. She had a colonoscopy 2 years ago that showed extensive diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. Her diet is low in fiber. She reports one episode of constipation followed by loose stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.8°F, heart rate 86, blood pressure 128/76. On examination, there is moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant with voluntary guarding but no rebound tenderness or rigidity. Bowel sounds are present and hypoactive. There is no palpable mass. Laboratory work shows a white blood cell count of 13,200 with a left shift. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.
